Message
mĕs´sāj
n. (a word sent by one person to another through a bearer; rendering Hebrew dabar and mal'akut, Greek aggelia and presbeia)
Old French message, from Latin missus, sent. A message is not the messenger's own; John's word for it, aggelia, is what an angel carries.

Biblical Definition

John twice names the content of the apostolic message: “This then is the message which we have heard of him, and declare unto you, that God is light, and in him is no darkness at all” (1Jn 1:5); and “this is the message that ye heard from the beginning, that we should love one another” (1Jn 3:11). Haggai was “the LORD's messenger in the LORD's message unto the people, saying, I am with you, saith the LORD” (Hag 1:13). Ehud told Eglon, “I have a message from God unto thee,” and it was a dagger (Jdg 3:20). The citizens in the parable “sent a message after him, saying, We will not have this man to reign over us” (Luk 19:14). “He that sendeth a message by the hand of a fool cutteth off the feet, and drinketh damage” (Pro 26:6).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines message as any notice, word, or communication, written or verbal, sent from one person to another.

expand to see more

MESSAGE, n. Any notice, word or communication, written or verbal, sent from one person to another.

2. An official written communication of facts or opinions sent by a chief magistrate to the two houses of a legislature.

Key Scripture

1Jn 1:5 — "This then is the message which we have heard of him, and declare unto you, that God is light, and in him is no darkness at all."

1Jn 3:11 — "For this is the message that ye heard from the beginning, that we should love one another."

Hag 1:13 — "Then spake Haggai the LORD'S messenger in the LORD'S message unto the people, saying, I am with you, saith the LORD."

Jdg 3:20 — "And Ehud came unto him; and he was sitting in a summer parlour, which he had for himself alone. And Ehud said, I have a message from God unto thee. And he arose out of his seat."

Luk 19:14 — "But his citizens hated him, and sent a message after him, saying, We will not have this man to reign over us."

Pro 26:6 — "He that sendeth a message by the hand of a fool cutteth off the feet, and drinketh damage."

Modern Corruption

The modern message begins with man's needs, and the apostle's message began with a sentence about God.

expand to see more

First John 1:5 is the first thing the apostles had to say, and it is not about the hearer. “This then is the message… that God is light, and in him is no darkness at all.” The felt-needs gospel opens with the man — his wounds, his potential, his search — and brings God in afterward as the answer to what the man was already asking. John opens with God's character, and everything that follows in the letter (walking in the light, confessing sin, the blood that cleanses) is the consequence of that one sentence. A message that starts anywhere else will end somewhere else.

The word itself is a correction. A message is carried, not composed; Haggai was the LORD's messenger in the LORD's message, and the whole of his authority was that the words were not his. The preacher who improves the message has become its author, and the citizens of Luke 19 show what men do with a message they dislike: they send one back. “We will not have this man to reign over us” is the reply of every generation to the announcement of a King, and the parable records what the King did when he returned.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew dabar (H1697), a word, matter; mal'akut (H4400), a message, errand; Greek aggelia (G31), a message, announcement; presbeia (G4242), an embassy.

expand to see more

Hebrew dabar (H1697) — word, message; Judges 3:20, 1 Kings 20:12, Proverbs 26:6.

Hebrew mal'akut (H4400) — a message, errand; Haggai 1:13 only.

Greek aggelia (G31) — message, announcement; 1 John 1:5, 3:11; presbeia (G4242), an embassy; Luke 19:14, 14:32.

Usage

"“This then is the message… that God is light” — the apostles' first sentence."

"“The LORD's messenger in the LORD's message” — carried, not composed."

"“Sent a message after him, saying, We will not have this man to reign over us” — the reply of the citizens."
